fields.tjmac\n\n 2014-11-06 03:55\n\nreporter:
I was pleasantly surprised that someone was looking at these bugs! It was beginning to look like a version 3.4.9 would never be released, and yet there are still a lot of bugs in this version. And there is no way that I can upgrade to 4.X because it's way to slow for my large database.

As for your above query:

Yes, all the detailed dates (ie ones with year, month, day) sort correctly. It's everything else, including dates without a day, that are not grouped consistently. It seems that the biggest problem is that there needs to be a routine that sorts the dates with alphanumeric characters (words) -- that would fix about 90% of the problem.

fields.tjmac\n\n 2015-11-01 03:06\n\nreporter:
This bug is still present in 4.2.1. I hate to keep writing about it, but it really bugs me. When I'm comparing 10 screens of people with the same birth year, and I have to scroll 10 pages up or down just because this isn't fixed.

You see, the modifier "after" should be places after all dates with that date.

eg.
person a before 1902
person b about 1902
person c 1902
person d jan 5, 1902
person...
Person x after 1902

Currently, person a, b, c, and x are found in any order! This example seems the most appropriate (logical) order for comparing people (which I do 50% of the time), because they are ordered as close as possible (position-wise) to a potential duplicate person with an exact date (a date that includes day,month,year).

UPDATE: Here is my suggestion on how the modifier "between" should be positioned/placed in a list -- an approximate average should be taken. I would be happy to see gramps just take the difference between the two years (eg. 1922 and 1933 = 10), divided by 2 (10/2), equaling earlier date plus result (1922+5=1927). So in this case it would be positioned before jan 1, 1927 or before/after dates with just the year 1927.

This above proposal could be used precisely if it didn't slow gramps down too much. Example: Betw Feb 9, 1853 and July 27, 1860, would be divided by two and added to the date Feb 9, 1853... the result would be placed in a precise avg date (so when seen, and comparing names, the user would know to look above and below the given "between" date.)
